entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Chremonides, an Athenian statesman and general active in the mid-3rd century BCE, rose to prominence as the architect of the Chremonidean War (267–261 BCE), a desperate, yet ultimately unsuccessful, attempt by several Greek city-states to break free from Macedonian hegemony. His significance lies in leading the last major concerted effort by Athens to reclaim its traditional independence against the rising power of the Antigonid dynasty, marking a critical juncture in the Hellenistic world where the autonomy of the polis was increasingly overshadowed by the successor kingdoms. This conflict involved major Hellenistic powers, notably Ptolemaic Egypt, which supported the Greek cause.

The core of Chremonides's policy was the formation of a pan-Hellenic alliance, primarily with Sparta, and crucially, securing the backing of Ptolemy II Philadelphus of Egypt. This coalition aimed to challenge the dominance of Antigonus II Gonatas, the Antigonid king of Macedon, who maintained garrisons in strategic locations like the Piraeus, effectively controlling Athens. Chremonides successfully passed a decree in 268 BCE, known as the Chremonidean Decree, which formalized this alliance and declared war. Despite initial Ptolemaic naval support, the allied land forces, including Spartan King Areus I, were decisively defeated by Antigonus at Corinth, and Athens itself endured a protracted siege from 266 to 262 BCE. The city, weakened by famine, eventually surrendered, leading to Chremonides's exile.
